title: The Future of New Technology and Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health: Prospects, Challenges, and a Roadmap for Personalized Treatment
description:
Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital technologies are rapidly entering mental health care, psychosomatic medicine, and psychotherapy. Yet the clinical value of these tools cannot be judged by technical performance alone. The field is characterized by diagnostic heterogeneity, reliance on language and self-report, complex biopsychosocial causation, and substantial variability in response to interventions. Clinically meaningful progress therefore requires integration of biological markers with patients’ lived experience, personal history and context, alongside person-centered precision decision-making and intervention.
Summary. This review examines how AI may contribute to mental health care across multiple levels, including diagnostic assessment, biomarker development, treatment selection, AI-enabled non-invasive neuromodulation, closed-loop adaptation, and emerging chatbot-based interventions. We argue that AI should support and improve, not replace, clinical assessments and care by integrating complex data into person-centered care, while raising challenges of validation, safety, equity, commodification and governance.
Key Messages. AI can strengthen and improve clinically effective, context-sensitive, and person-centered mental health care. AI may enhance diagnosis, treatment selection, and therapeutic options while preserving the human-human therapeutic alliance. The future of AI-enabled mental health depends on combining computational precision with human judgment, ethical oversight, and clinical relevance to improve patient outcomes and quality of life. 
Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Mental health; Personalized treatment; Psychotherapy; Psychosomatic medicine

title: Understanding Refugee Parent-Child Discrepancies in Reporting Socio-Emotional Well-Being
description: Canada has welcomed over 100,000 Syrian refugees since 2015, many of whom have faced displacement-related challenges that shape their socio-emotional well-being. Refugee children, in particular, are at heightened risk for socio-emotional difficulties due to their developmental sensitivity to adversity, exposure to traumatic events, and resettlement stressors. Assessing children’s socio-emotional well-being often relies on both parent-reports and child self-reports; however, discrepancies between these reports commonly occur, and the factors influencing such discrepancies are not well understood, particularly in displaced populations. The present study examined predictors of parent-child discrepancies in reports of socio-emotional well-being and explored whether such discrepancies were associated with children’s learning outcomes. Participants were Syrian refugee children (N = 55, Mage = 14.42) who were resettled in Canada for an average of six years. Results revealed that children consistently self-reported more socio-emotional problems than their parents reported. Moreover, longer time resettled in Canada predicted greater parent-child discrepancies, suggesting that resettlement-related factors and acculturation influence parent-child discrepancies. However, child self-reports, but not parent-reports, showed limited external validity; while parent-child communication barriers may contribute to discrepancies, differences in how socio-emotional constructs are understood and reported by parents and children are important to consider. These findings underscore the importance of including multiple informants in socio-emotional well-being assessments and carefully considering cultural and contextual factors when designing assessments, specifically given the complex dynamics in displaced families. title: Cognitive Feelings from Healthy Experience to Psychopathology: An Integrative Review Across Phenomenology, Psychology, Neuroscience, and Computation
description: Cognitive feelings, such as the feeling of knowing, familiarity, presence, reality, confidence, agency, and body ownership, are subjective experiences arising from cognitive processes, playing crucial roles in perception, memory, and decision-making. Despite extensive research across philosophy, psychology, and neuroscience, they have been studied in fragmented ways, lacking a unified theoretical framework. This review integrates multiple perspectives on cognitive feelings. First, we catalog fifteen cognitive feelings organized in thirteen subsections, examining their normal functions and clinical manifestations when disrupted. Second, drawing on the phenomenological tradition from William James through Husserl and Heidegger to Ratcliffe, we distinguish three modes of cognitive feelings: feelings of thought (metacognitive monitoring), feelings of perception (constitution of worldly appearances), and feelings of being (existential self–world relations). Third, from the perspective of affective psychology, we demonstrate that cognitive feelings share neural substrates with emotions, particularly the anterior insular cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, and are bidirectionally modulated by mood states. Fourth, from a neurological perspective, we extend Damasio’s somatic marker hypothesis to cognitive feelings as metacognitive somatic markers, whose selective disruption through right-hemisphere damage produces characteristic monothematic delusions, suggesting hemispheric asymmetries. Fifth, we present a computational framework based on predictive processing theory, explaining cognitive feelings through prediction errors, precision weighting, and free energy minimization. Across these perspectives, we examine impairments in psychiatric and neurological disorders, including depersonalization, schizophrenia, Capgras syndrome, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, and depression, bridging theory with clinical observation.

title: Targeting Emotion Coping Beliefs in Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial of An Online Single-Session Intervention
description: Objective: Traditional psychological interventions pose various access barriers related to time, geography, provider availability, and cost. Online, self-directed single-session interventions (SSIs) can mitigate such access barriers. However, SSI effect sizes are highly heterogenous. Targeting core transdiagnostic processes may improve SSI consistency. This randomized controlled trial (registration NCT07034027 via clinicaltrials.gov) evaluated a novel SSI targeting the transdiagnostic construct of emotion coping beliefs. Method: Participants aged 18-29 reporting deficits in emotional nonreactivity abilities (N = 550) were randomized to the SSI condition or the control and completed questionnaires assessing emotion intolerance beliefs and related constructs at baseline, post-activity, and two-week follow-up. Multilevel modeling was used to assess differential proximal and distal change in emotion intolerance beliefs. Participants in the SSI condition also provided ratings of perceived intervention teaching effectiveness. Results: The first hypothesis — that proximal reductions in emotional intolerance beliefs would be greater for SSI participants than for control participants — was supported at p < 0.001, with a near-medium Cohen’s d effect size derived from a standard regression. This differential benefit was not sustained at follow-up. The second hypothesis — that participants would self-report the activity “somewhat” helped them learn to be nonreactive — was not clearly supported, as the mean rating was slightly below the preregistered cutoff. However, participants provided positive views of the intervention. Conclusions: The SSI appears promising as a highly scalable on-demand tool for acute distress accompanied by low coping self-efficacy. Future efforts should examine the conditions under which acute benefits might be sustained.

title: It's Not a Bug, It's a Feature: Agentic and Relational Needs as Two Alliance Pathways for AI Mental Health Tools
description: Can artificial intelligence be a therapist? The answer depends on what kind of help the person needs. AI mental health tools generate responses perceived as empathic, yet their value drops when users learn the source is artificial. This pattern has entrenched a default assumption: AI's non-human nature is a deficit to be corrected. We argue that this assumption rests on two errors: the belief that therapy is fundamentally about the relational bond, and the treatment of AI's non-human nature as a limitation rather than a resource. We propose a reframe organized around psychological needs. Relational needs (connection, belonging, acceptance) anchor a Relational Alliance, where AI is structurally limited. Agentic needs (autonomy, competence, self-efficacy) anchor an Agentic Alliance, where that same non-human nature may be a feature: a private workspace for self-directed growth rather than a failed simulation of human care. Converging evidence supports this separation: AI-generated responses make people feel heard but not connected once the source is disclosed; a supportive chatbot designed using relationship science fails to reduce loneliness beyond journaling, although a random human stranger succeeds; and the mechanisms linking AI tools to well-being run through self-efficacy and perceived autonomy rather than felt connection. This reframe carries concrete implications for how large language model (LLM)-based tools are prompted, how therapeutic process is evaluated computationally, and what outcome metrics count as success. The question shifts from “How humanly good is AI?” to “Which needs does this tool address, through what mechanisms, and for whom?”

title: The associations between rumination and depression in late adolescence: a longitudinal study using the IMAGEN adolescent cohort
description:
Background
Depression is a leading cause of global disease burden, yet effective prevention strategies remain limited. Identifying targetable risk factors is therefore a priority. Rumination, a style of repetitive negative thinking, has been linked to depression and anxiety, but has traditionally been viewed a symptom of depressive episodes rather than a cognitive vulnerability. Moreover, previous studies have not consistently addressed key confounders such as anxiety or the possibility of reverse causality. This study aimed to examine the longitudinal and bidirectional associations between rumination and depression in adolescents.

Methods
Participants were drawn from the IMAGEN adolescent cohort. Depression was assessed using the Development and Wellbeing Assessment (DAWBA), and rumination using the Ruminative Responses Scale (RRS), at ages 18 and 22. Bidirectional longitudinal associations were examined using logistic and linear regression models. Analyses were conducted unadjusted and adjusted for a range of confounders, including baseline symptoms and anxiety.

Results 
Complete data were available for 800 adolescents (59.66% female, 40.12% male, mean age at first time point 18.42 years, SD=0.67). Higher rumination at age 18 was associated with depression at age 22, including after adjustment for confounders (adjusted OR=1.45, 95% CI 1.14–1.86, P=0.003). In contrast, there was no evidence that depression at age 18 was associated with rumination at age 22 after adjustment (mean difference = -0.52, 95% CI -1.69–0.64, P=0.379).

Conclusion
Overall, these findings indicate that rumination is associated with later depression from late adolescence into early adulthood, independent of baseline symptoms and confounders, with no evidence of reverse effects. This supports rumination as a vulnerability marker and a potential target for prevention, although intervention studies are needed to test causal effects.

title: Autistic student well-being indicators at school: Parent, educator and therapist perspectives
description: Autistic students experience disproportionately high levels of distress and unmet support needs at school, yet there is limited school‑based evidence to guide how their well‑being is recognised in everyday educational contexts. Most existing research has focused on home, community, or clinical settings, leaving a gap in understanding how autistic students communicate both high and low well‑being during the school day. This study addresses this gap by increasing understanding of school‑based indicators of autistic student well‑being across emotional, social, physical, academic, and future‑focused domains. Using a two‑phase, multi-informant design, Phase 1 collected qualitative data from caregivers, educators, and school‑based therapists (n = 41) to identify externally observable indicators of high and low well‑being. Phase 2 invited a separate sample (n = 36) to evaluate the perceived reliability of the most frequently identified indicators. Inductive content analysis identified 94 high and 99 low well‑being indicators. Three key findings emerged. First, indicators varied substantially in how they were expressed across students, highlighting the importance of interpreting change relative to individual baselines rather than normative expectations. Second, many indicators reflected specific dimensions of well‑being and did not function as global markers across contexts. Third, indicators most frequently reported were not always those judged to be most reliable indicators of autistic students’ well-being, underscoring the limitations of frequency‑based approaches. Together, these findings demonstrate that autistic student well‑being at school is best understood as multidimensional, context‑dependent, and individually patterned. title: From Maternal Depression to Autism Risk: Shared Neurobiological Mechanisms Across the Perinatal Period
description:
Perinatal depression (PND) is a subtype of major depressive disorder with onset during the peripartum
period or up to one year after childbirth in clinical practice. It is the most prevalent complication
during the postpartum period with a global prevalence between 10-20%. Emerging research has
shown that PND can exert long term effects on child development through the disruption of both
biological signaling (e.g., oxytocinergic and GABAergic system dysfunction, HPA axis dysregulation
and inflammatory state) and maternal-infant social bonding. These disruptions have been linked to
adverse cognitive, social, and behavioural outcomes, including impaired emotional attachment.
Consequently, there is an increasing imperative to evaluate the potential association between maternal
PND and the development of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in offspring, particularly in light of the
rising global prevalence, mostly due to higher awareness and increased diagnostic recognition.
While recent literature has explored this association using mainly observational prospective studies, a
comprehensive synthesis of the evidence is currently lacking. This review aims to analyze available
literature regarding the association between PND and the development of ASD in the offspring,
focusing primarily on a possibly shared pathophysiology, which includes alterations in the
oxytocinergic and GABAergic system together with epigenetic changes and the inflammatory profile.

title: A Markov Chain Monte Carlo Procedure with Simulated Annealing for Shortening Assessments
description: Symptom screeners, patient assessments, and cognitive tests are used to measure constructs such as health-related quality of life, levels of mental health symptoms, and ability. The items are often summarized, through a simple unweighted sum score or through more advanced methods, including factor analysis, Rasch modeling, and item response theory. However, long instruments increase respondent burden and it may be desirable to shorten them. One consideration that is often overlooked is that in many contexts, these instruments are used less for precise measurement of a latent construct but instead for accurate prediction of a diagnosis, expert judgment, or classification. As such, we present a method to shorten instruments that prioritizes reproduction of expert judgment based on an unweighted sum score through the use of a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm with simulated annealing to explore the search space of potential short forms. This method is orders of magnitude more efficient than brute force search and has the advantage of optimizing for prediction of the desired outcome directly, instead of optimizing on the measurement of an intermediate outcome that may not be perfectly aligned with the decision criteria of interest. We prove the correctness of the algorithm, demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency through simulation studies, and apply it to a screener for alcohol use disorder, demonstrating that under the unweighted sum score scoring constraint, shortened forms can more accurately predict expert judgments than full forms.

title: Cord Blood C-Reactive Protein and ADHD Symptoms at Age 5: Evidence from Two French Birth Cohorts
description:

Background: Conditions associated with perinatal inflammation have been identified as risk factors for neurodevelopmental disorders, including Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). However, data linking early inflammatory biomarkers with later ADHD symptoms remain scarce. The acute phase C-reactive protein (CRP) is a key marker of systemic inflammation. To date, no studies have examined the association between CRP levels in cord blood (reflecting neonatal inflammation) and subsequent childhood ADHD symptoms. Here, we aimed to investigate whether elevated cord blood CRP concentrations are associated with child’s ADHD symptoms at age 5. 
Methods: We analyzed data from 1019 and 831 mother–child pairs enrolled in the ELFE and EDEN prospective birth cohorts, respectively. CRP levels in cord blood were measured using an immunoassay. ADHD symptoms were assessed at age 5 using the hyperactivity–inattention subscale of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Outcomes included both continuous scores and categorical thresholds: borderline (≥6) and abnormal (≥7) hyperactivity–inattention symptoms. title: Computational mechanisms behind the vicious cycle of aversive beliefs and avoidance
description:
Heightened threat beliefs and avoidance are core symptoms of anxiety-related psychopathology. Yet, how beliefs drive avoidance and whether avoidance in turn prevents those beliefs from being updated remains unclear. Here, we tested this bidirectional relationship in N=236 participants using a gamified aversive learning and spatial navigation task in which participants rated threat before and after making costly avoidance decisions. We combined behavioural analyses with computational modelling to quantify threat generalisation, avoidance, and their association with transdiagnostic symptom dimensions derived from self-report measures.
Participants generalised threat to nearby locations, and higher location-specific threat beliefs predicted subsequent avoidance. In turn, avoidance shaped belief updating: visiting a location reduced threat beliefs even in the absence of location-specific feedback, whereas avoiding a location preserved them. We find that individuals scoring high on a transdiagnostic symptom dimension capturing worry and Intolerance of Uncertainty are overall more avoidant and that this behaviour was best explained by increased threat beliefs, not a general tendency to avoid more. 
In this work we identify a bidirectional link between beliefs and behaviour in aversive decision-making and show that maladaptive avoidance arises from how threat is inferred and generalized. These findings identify a self-reinforcing cycle, in which threat beliefs guide avoidance and avoidance prevents those beliefs from being revised, which may be a critical contributor to the maintenance of pathological anxiety.

title: The TEA Nets framework combines AI and cognitive network science to model targets, events and actors in text
description: We introduce Target-Event-Agent Networks (TEA Nets) as a computational framework to extract subjects (``Agents"), verbs (``Events"), and objects (``Targets") from texts. Grounded in cognitive network science and artificial intelligence, TEA Nets are implemented as an open-source Python library. We test TEA Nets in three case studies, demonstrating the framework's ability to perform interpretable emotion detection, semantic frame analyses, and linguistic inquiries across conspiracy texts and textual responses generated by LLMs. In the LOCO conspiracy corpus, TEA Nets revealed that highly conspiratorial narratives (4,227 texts) linked personal pronouns (``I", ``you", ``we") with the same actions twice as frequently as low-similarity conspiracy narratives. High-conspiracy narratives connected person-focused elements (``you", ``people") through actions eliciting anger above the random baseline ($z = 2.63, p < .05$), a trend absent in low-similarity conspiracy narratives, which emphasized scientific actors (``researcher", ``scientist"). In the HOPE and CounseLLMe datasets of 212 (human) and 200 (LLM-based) psychotherapy transcripts, respectively, TEA Nets highlighted emotional differences. When expressing feelings, Claude 3 Haiku, GPT-3.5, and humans used sad words with higher frequency than random expectations but Haiku expressed sadness with lower emotional intensity than humans ($U = 1243.5, p = .036$). We discuss these differences in the context of psychotherapy training on LLM-simulated patients. Our results show that Target-Event-Agent Networks can extract relevant emotional, syntactic, and semantic insights from narratives, opening new avenues for text analysis with cognitive network science.

title: 1000 Days of HRV: A Case Study of Daily Post-Wake-Up Heart Rate Variability for Tracking Stressful Life Events
description: Longitudinal monitoring of heart rate variability (HRV) can offer deep insight into an individualized physiological trajectory of responding to stressful events. The current single-participant longitudinal case study (male, 26 to 29 years; N = 1) reports 1,000 days of post-wake-up resting-state HRV recordings, complemented by 878 nights of nocturnal HRV and 142 diary entries documenting noteworthy events. The study examined (1) whether daily post-wake-up HRV can identify meaningful within-person physiological deviations that correspond to naturally occurring stressful periods or impactful events, (2) whether shorter 1-minute recordings are equally informative compared with full 2-minute recordings, and (3) how post-wake-up and nocturnal HRV relate. Thirteen downward deviations from the typical range were identified, most of which corresponded to meaningful contextual life events. The largest reduction in HRV occurred during a period of exposure to a war zone, concurrent respiratory illness, and bereavement. Other pronounced HRV suppressions were observed during psychologically stressful periods or medical conditions, including two benign paroxysmal positional vertigo episodes. RMSSD derived from 1-minute versus 2-minute recordings showed close agreement (r = .92, p < .001), suggesting that shorter recordings may provide similar information. In contrast, post-wake-up and nocturnal RMSSD showed only modest correspondence (r = .35, p < .001), with nocturnal HRV appearing less sensitive to contextual changes. These findings suggest that a brief, standardized post-wake-up HRV protocol can feasibly capture meaningful day-to-day physiological dynamics in everyday life, relative to one’s own typical range, helping investigate individualized trajectories of stress response, recovery, and adaptation.

title: Social camouflaging among autistic adolescents in Japan: Diﬀerential associations with aﬃliate stigma reported by mothers and fathers
description:
Autistic adolescentsʼ use of social camouflaging, defined as strategies used to appear less visibly
autistic during social interaction, has been increasingly recognised by researchers, but its
developmental and family context remains poorly understood. Aﬃliate stigma, experienced by family
members because of their association with an autistic person, and internalised stigma, reflecting the
incorporation of negative societal beliefs about autism into oneʼs self-concept, may be relevant
correlates. Using an online questionnaire survey of 50 autistic adolescent‒mother‒father triads, this
study examined whether parental aﬃliate stigma was associated with autistic adolescentsʼ
internalised stigma and, in turn, with social camouflaging, while comparing maternal and paternal
pathways. Adolescents reported social camouflaging and internalised stigma, and parents reported
aﬃliate stigma. Path analysis showed that autistic adolescentsʼ internalised stigma was positively
associated with social camouflaging. Both maternal and paternal aﬃliate stigma were positively
associated with adolescentsʼ internalised stigma, but neither was directly associated with social
camouflaging. In the simultaneous model, only the paternal path remained independently associated
with adolescentsʼ internalised stigma.

title: Developmental and environmental differences in the first year of life of infants with family history of autism and/or ADHD in Brazil
description: Prospective longitudinal studies have established that infants with family history (FH) of autism or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are likely to experience a range of differences in their early development. However, the vast majority of evidence concerning the early development of these infants has come from high-income-country (HIC) contexts and has not considered the role of psychosocial environmental factors. In this study, we investigated developmental and environmental differences in a large cohort (N=252) of infants aged 6-12 months (mean=8.7 months) with FH of autism (n=36), ADHD (n=66), autism and ADHD (n=84) or without FH (n=66) in a low-and-middle-income-country (LMIC) setting, Brazil. Infants with FH of autism showed significantly lower adaptive communication, motor and daily living skills as well as lower temperamental perceptual sensitivity and vocal reactivity than infants without FH of autism (F>4.18, p<0.04), while infants with FH of ADHD showed significantly higher temperamental activity levels and lower temperamental regulatory capacity than infants without FH of ADHD (F>9.23, p<0.003). Compared to infants without FH, infants with FH of autism and/or FH of ADHD had significantly higher levels of caregiver mental health difficulties and household chaos (F>7.91, p<0.005). Our findings suggest distinct profiles of developmental differences associated with FH of autism versus FH of ADHD and shared environmental vulnerabilities in the home. This work highlights the importance of providing support for infants with FH of autism and ADHD and their families in Brazil.

title: Recognizing the Need for Creativity: Correlates of Unfulfilled Creative Needs at Work
description: Creativity is widely recognized as a driver of organizational innovation, yet employees’ own need for creativity remains understudied. This study examined both the prevalence and perceived importance of the need for creativity in the workplace, as well as the unique associations between unfulfilled creative needs and indicators of well-being and professional life satisfaction. A total of 251 French-speaking employees were recruited online from a diverse range of industries and companies of varying sizes. Two novel dimensions, i.e. freedom to be creative and perceived receptivity of the work environment to creativity, were incorporated into the Pathways to Quality of Life at Work®. Findings revealed that these creativity-related dimensions were rated as relatively important, ranking alongside advancement opportunities, benefits, and collegial relationships. Stronger creative dispositions, measured using a composite score based on creative self-beliefs and achievements, were associated with a greater reported need for creativity but were not significantly related to unfulfilled creative needs—defined as the gap between desired and actual levels of creativity in the workplace. In contrast, unfulfilled creative needs were uniquely associated with elevated mental health symptoms and lower professional life satisfaction, even after controlling for creative dispositions and unfulfilled needs in other key domains identified as important by participants (i.e., working schedule, income level and security, communication efficiency, opportunities for advancement, social benefits, healthy work environment and autonomy). These findings highlight the importance of incorporating creativity-related dimensions into assessments of quality of work life and further emphasize the benefits of cultivating organizational and managerial environments that actively recognize and support employees’ creative needs.

title: From the Social to the Individual: Human Interdependence Calls for Explanatory Reversal in Mind and Brain
description: Recent years have witnessed an “interactive turn” in the cognitive sciences, increasingly foregrounding real-time social interaction and organism–environment dynamics. Yet, even the interactive turn often stops short of its own implications, leaving an individual-first explanatory order largely intact. Taking these implications seriously points toward an explanatory reversal: human interdependence is primary, and individual cognition emerges within—and remains dependent upon—relational dynamics. In this review article, selectively drawing on philosophy of mind, developmental psychology, social neuroscience, neurophysiology and neuroecology, we set out a social-first perspective in which regulation, vulnerability, and agency are shaped through histories of affective, behavioral, and physiological co-regulation, including patterns of attunement, misattunement, and repair. Using interpersonal synchrony as a diagnostic case, we argue that recent work makes it increasingly feasible to treat synchrony not only as a statistical marker of coordination, but as an entry point for analysing interactional organization and its effects on individual cognition across causal, directional, and multiscale dimensions. In this regard, we synthesize findings indicating that interpersonal coordination can shape not only social outcomes but also apparently individual processes, motivating closer attention to social-to-individual pathways across scales. Making these commitments explicit supports an explanatory reversal that proceeds from the social to the individual, initiating a shift from documenting covariation to explaining how interaction reorganizes cognition across minds, bodies, and environments. We conclude by drawing out the implications of this shift for theory, empirical research, artificial intelligence, and societal practice.

title: Decision Outcomes for Ill-Structured Problems in Top Management Teams: mapping Facilitators and Barriers in a Scoping Review
description: Top Management Teams (TMTs) of many organizations struggle with ill-structured problems due to volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous environments. Our objective was to obtain insight into facilitators and barriers contributing to decisions in ill-structured problem settings. A scoping review following the Prisma-SCR protocol was conducted, resulting in 39 included studies. The most investigated decision outcomes were decision quality, decision commitment and decision effectiveness. Facilitators were (1) behavioral integration; (2) procedural rationality; (3) task conflict and (4) trust. Relationship conflict was a barrier. Political behavior, (team) leadership and diversity can either be a facilitator, a barrier or a secondary predictor. Perhaps most surprisingly is what we did not find: the role of emotions during decision making. Affect is underexposed in empirical research about team decision-making. Our findings suggest that decision outcomes are shaped by a complex interaction between primary and secondary predictors. Future research may expose how barriers and facilitators jointly affect the various types of decision outcomes, also over time. Moreover, we recommend more attention for behavioral integration and conflict mitigation. Lastly, the role of emotions should be incorporated within research designs about top level decision-making.

title: New Voices for Environmental Causes – The Psychological Basis of Different Reactions to Posts by Human and Virtual Greenfluencers
description:
Despite the growing presence of Virtual Influencers (VIs) and their potentially far-reaching impacts, their socio-political effects remain underexplored. The present paper provides the first systematic investigation of audience reactions to posts by human versus virtual greenfluencers. Drawing on persuasion research and Social Identity Theory, we hypothesized that posts by human versus virtual influencers and gender-congruent influencers are rated as more credible and that these variables may also be linked to engagement. Furthermore, we expected that trust in humans and AI are positively related to the perceived credibility of posts of the respective influencer type. We examined relations with engagement exploratorily.
In a 3×2-mixed online experiment, N = 410 participants were presented either with posts by (i) AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers, (ii) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, or (iii) human greenfluencers. Each participant further saw posts by a greenfluencer depicting (i) a man and (ii) a woman. Participants self-reported perceived credibility and engagement intentions with each post. 
Results show that while gender congruency had no significant effects, participants rated human greenfluencer posts as most credible and showed higher engagement with them compared to posts by both virtual greenfluencer types. Trust in AI emerged as a relevant but nuanced predictor of the different outcomes for different greenfluencer types.
As virtual influencers become more prevalent, differences in reactions to them versus human influencers may attenuate. Given their scalability, it thus remains important to examine when and for whom virtual political influencers and their posts may elicit comparable or even stronger reactions than human influencers.

title: Uncertainty mindset intervention promotes uncertainty-as-enabling beliefs and modulates directed exploration
description: Uncertainty is prevalent in everyday decision-making and lies at the heart of the explore-exploit dilemma. Prior work has shown that psychological constructs related to uncertainty processing are associated with individual differences in exploration. Yet, it remains unclear whether interventions targeting beliefs about uncertainty can influence how people explore. In a randomized controlled study (total N = 862), we administered a brief ~10-min uncertainty mindset intervention designed to promote the perspective that uncertainty offers opportunities and can be actively shaped by individual action, and examined whether it influences uncertainty-driven exploration. The intervention increased uncertainty-as-enabling mindsets and improved affective and cognitive outcomes relative to a control group. Using computational models of different exploration strategies, we demonstrated that although the intervention did not uniformly increase the tendency to explore uncertain options, it strengthened the association between uncertainty-as-enabling mindsets and directed exploration. These findings suggest that a brief, easily scalable intervention can enhance the extent to which uncertainty-related beliefs guide exploratory behaviour, with broader implications for well-being and adaptive functioning under uncertainty.

title: Key Processes Supporting Engagement and Impact in a School-Based, Indicated Preventative Mental Health Programme: A Qualitative Study of Young People’s Perspectives
description:
Background
Increasing evidence suggests that embedding accessible, preventative mental health support within schools can play a key role in addressing rising rates of mental health difficulties in adolescence. Understanding young people’s perspectives is essential to examine whether these new approaches are acceptable and engaging, and to understand conditions that limit or contribute to effective delivery.
Methods
Semi-structured interviews (n=87) were conducted with students who participated in a randomised controlled trial evaluating a new targeted preventative mental health intervention for adolescents, the ReSET Programme. Interviews were digitally transcribed and then analysed using Framework Analysis.
Results
Analysis identified four sequential, interconnected processes as fundamental to engagement in the programme and experiencing benefit beyond the group: 1) Creating a psychologically safe, youth-owned space, 2) Building peer connection to enhance engagement, 3) Learning together through practical activities, and 4) Establishing confidence and applying competencies. 
Conclusions
These findings have practical implications for delivery of ReSET and offer valuable evidence to support the wider integration of preventative, group-based mental health provision in schools. The perspectives of young people offer critical guidance on the conditions that facilitate or limit engagement and impact, underscoring the value of embedding their insights to enhance programme relevance and implementation.

title: Media Selectivity Research in Light of Self-Defeating Tendencies: Towards a Novel Understanding of Media Effects on Well-Being
description: A critical gap persists in media uses and effects research: while existing work has predominantly focused on self-serving motivations for media selection, an expanding body of evidence suggests that individuals—including those with psychological vulnerabilities—may seek out online content that aggravates, rather than alleviates, distress. Drawing on scholarship on self-defeating tendencies in offline contexts, we argue that the same process may unfold in mediated environments, especially on social media: when negative self-concepts are salient, users may gravitate toward content that validates these self-views, even at the expense of their well-being. We focus on mental health content as an illustrative case in which these dynamics become particularly visible and harmful, while arguing that similar processes apply to other domains. To guide this line of inquiry and offer a more comprehensive account of media selection processes and their implications for well-being, we extend the established Selective Exposure Self- and Affect-Management (SESAM) model by incorporating self-defeating motivations and outline a research agenda.

title: Perceived time and effort in physical activity and exercise  behavior
description: Humans perceive time and effort as scarce resources and often act to conserve them. This is reflected in a preference for brief over sustained effort, and for immediate outcomes over delayed ones. In physical activity contexts, people can choose between activities with different time and effort demands, such as taking the stairs versus the escalator or biking versus walking to work. Exercise makes this especially salient: People can choose options that require little time but induce high momentary effort costs (e.g., high-intensity interval training) and options that require less momentary effort but more time (e.g., low-intensity aerobic training). Although temporal and effort discounting have been studied extensively in isolation, how people jointly integrate these costs in physical activity and exercise contexts remains underexplored. Here, we propose that perceived time and effort should be considered jointly as experiential costs that modulate exercise decisions, regulation and persistence. Because effort and time rarely accrue independently, we synthesize limited and indirect evidence from movement-related decision-making, motor control, and exercise research to illustrate how people may trade off these costs when selecting between effort-time configurations. Furthermore, we review evidence that perceived effort can affect how time is experienced during exercise, and discuss factors that moderate this relationship. Taken together, this perspective offers a conceptual framework for studying how people balance effort and time when choosing and sustaining physical activity and exercise behavior. By clarifying key concepts and their interplay, we aim to support future work on effort-time costs and new questions for basic and applied research.

title: Expertise, Numeracy, and AI Trust in Financial Decision Making: When Calculation Strategies Meet Deliberation Time
description:
Financial decision-making is increasingly influenced by external advice, raising questions about how individuals calibrate trust in human experts versus artificial intelligence. To make decisions consistent with normative standards like Expected Value (EV) in monetary lotteries, individuals must actively perform calculations rather than relying on intuitive heuristics. However, cognitive limitations such as low objective numeracy or cognitive depletion often hinder their ability to execute these analytical strategies.
This study tested whether brief instructional interventions, framed by different authoritative sources, could enhance financial decision-making in monetary lotteries. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: Control, General Introduction, Expert, or AI. In the Control condition, participants made choices across 40 monetary lotteries without strategic guidance. In the other conditions, participants received identical instructions on computing EV prior to the task. These instructions were presented either neutrally (General Introduction), framed as advice from a human economist (Expert), or framed as a strategy from a personalized algorithm (AI).
Results indicated that the general interventions did not universally increase EV-consistent choices compared to the Control group. However, important nuanced interactions emerged. Deliberation time mediated the relationship between the Expert condition and EV-consistent choices, as participants motivated by human authority slowed down to evaluate options. Conversely, high perceived objectivity in the AI condition actively suppressed task performance, suggesting an automation bias where unwarranted trust replaced analytical verification. Furthermore, higher objective numeracy positively correlated with normative choices, but its benefits were fully realized only by participants who maintained cognitive endurance throughout the task.

title: Empirical Findings on the Accuracy of Intellectual Self-Perceptions Depend on the Method Used to Assess Self-Perceived Ability
description: Research on people’s tendencies to over-, under-, or accurately estimate their abilities relies on assessments of self-perceived ability. Here, we investigated how the choice of an assessment method influences the conclusions drawn in research on two perspectives on accuracy. First, studies using the rank-order perspective are concerned with the correlation between self-perceived ability and an objective measure of “real” ability across individuals. Second, studies using the level perspective view the discrepancy between a person’s levels of self-perceived and real ability as an indicator of the degree of bias (vs. accuracy) and investigate the average discrepancy across people, individual differences in people’s discrepancies, or the association between the individual discrepancies and some outcome variable. In a cross-sectional survey of 281 participants, we assessed self-perceived intelligence in two domains (vocabulary knowledge, reasoning ability) with three measures each (percentile rank, IQ score, number of correct items). “Real” ability was measured with objective tests and transformed to match the scales of the self-assessments. We found that the measure for self-perceived intelligence impacted the conclusions drawn in analyses within the level but not the rank-order perspective. We discuss implications for the robustness of past findings and for the assessment of self-perceived intelligence in future studies.

title: Belief in a Just World and Deception Detection Accuracy: Two Unsuccessful Conceptual Replications of Schindler and Reinhard (2015)
description: The current paper presents conceptual replication attempts of Schindler and Reinhard (2015), who found a negative association between belief in a just world (BJW) — the positive illusion that the world is a just and orderly place — and deception detection accuracy. Two studies, one with undergraduates (Study 1 N = 176) and the other with members of the general public (Study 2 N = 352), failed to obtain this negative relationship and instead found a null effect. Exploratory analyses observed that in the general public sample, BJW was positively associated with truth-bias (one’s tendency to ascribe a message as honest independent of its actual veracity) and both raw and signal detection theory metrics produced consistent results. In sum, individual differences like belief in a just world are faint and generally unrelated to deception detection accuracy at least in the current research settings, though future work would benefit from boundary condition testing.

title: Inoculating against microtargeted political advertising: A personal values perspective
description: Political microtargeting, the tailoring of political messages to individuals based on their personal characteristics, poses risks to democratic decision-making. Previous research has shown that prompting individuals to reflect on their personality traits can enhance recognition of personality-based targeting. The present studies extend this approach to personal values, which are stronger predictors of political orientation and voting behaviour. Across three experiments with 1,247 British participants, we tested whether boosting interventions that encourage reflection on value priorities improve recognition of value-based political microtargeting. Using validated real-world political advertisements, we found that boosting increased participants’ ability to identify when ads matched their values and sharpened their sensitivity to mismatches. Although results varied across individual studies, internal meta-analyses confirmed significant overall effects for both recognition of matched ads and discrimination of mismatched ads. These findings provide the first empirical evidence that value-based boosting interventions can strengthen recognition of political microtargeting.

title: Limited evidence that reputation-based partner choice facilitates information sharing in humans
description: A necessary prerequisite for the accumulation of beneficial knowledge, or ‘cumulative cultural evolution’, is the sharing of information via social learning. Yet little work in the field of cultural evolution has examined the mechanisms that support information sharing in the face of exploitative information free-riding and information hoarding. We ran a series of online interactive experiments (N=716) combined with computational reinforcement and social learning models to test whether the mechanism of reputation-based partner choice can effectively support information sharing. Participants in groups chose whether to (i) engage in costly innovation and (ii) whether to share the resultant knowledge. Sharers received increased reputations for sharing and participants could use reputations to select recipients of knowledge. We found strong priors for information sharing that persisted throughout the experiments in participants from both the UK and China (Study 1). However, partner choice was generally too weak to explain the presence of widespread information sharing, which persisted even when we reduced the benefit of innovation (Study 2), introduced exploitative bots (Study 3), and removed reputations altogether (Study 4). Our results suggest that indiscriminate, group-based sharing is more important for facilitating cumulative cultural evolution than discriminate, reputation-based sharing.

title: From Green to Technology:  Age Group Variability in Conceptual Complexity and Concreteness
description:
Concepts are widely recognized as flexible and shaped by multiple factors. Here, we investigate how conceptual representations differ across age groups by focusing on four timely domains—ecological, geo, natural (which we labeled altogether green), and technological. Replicating a previous study, we collected ratings from 320 Italian older adults (aged >64) on 50 concepts per domain across 39 semantic dimensions targeting different conceptual aspects (e.g., sensorimotor, sociopolitical, inner, emotional). We then compared these ratings with those from younger adults (aged 18–35) collected in the earlier study.
Results revealed strong semantic proximity among green concepts and a clear separation between them (especially natural) and the technological ones. The internal semantic composition of each domain revealed clear age group differences. Within the green domains, older adults exhibited richer, more multifaceted, and more concrete conceptual representations than younger adults, with fine-grained divergences across green concepts. In contrast, no age group differences emerged in the complexity of technological concept representations; however, younger adults characterized this domain more concretely.
These differences were closely linked to self-reported domain experience and familiarity: older adults reported greater personal experience with ecological topics, whereas younger adults reported higher familiarity with technology.
Theoretically, our findings suggest that conceptual complexity and concreteness vary across domains and are shaped by age group membership and all that it entails. Scientifically, the resulting O-TECo database provides the first semantic norms tailored to older adults. Societally, results highlight the need for age-sensitive interventions to foster engagement with environmental policies and responsible technology use.

title: The wurst case scenario: A pictorial intervention to change the appeal of meat-based dishes.
description:
Background: Overconsumption of meat negatively impacts both the environment and human health, yet global meat consumption continues to rise. Therefore, effective and easily implementable interventions are needed to encourage reductions in meat consumption. This study builds on prior research suggesting that exposure to depictions of farm animals in positive, free-range, natural settings may reduce the desire to eat meat.
Methods: Participants completed a visual search task requiring them to distinguish between images of meat-based and vegan dishes. Before this task, participants were randomly assigned to two groups and exposed to images of either cows/pigs (intervention) or cats/dogs (control group). Self-reported desire to eat meat, reaction times and response errors were recorded for images of meat-based dishes.
Results: Exposure to images of cows and pigs reduced visual attention to meat-based dishes more than exposure to cats and dogs. The desire to eat meat was not reduced. On the contrary, there was a trend in the opposite direction with an increase in meat appetite.
Discussion: Participants may have perceived the animals as symbols of cruelty-free farming practices, reducing ethical concerns and potentially justifying meat consumption.

title: Social Capital, Socioeconomic Status, and Depression and Anxiety Among Young People in Latin America: A Case-Control Study
description:
Introduction. Growing evidence suggests that social capital is protective against common mental disorders, but how this affects adolescents and young adults living in highly deprived contexts outside of the Global North has received less attention. We investigated whether cognitive (i.e. trust, values) and structural (i.e. networks, support) social capital were associated with depression and anxiety in young people growing up in the poorest half of three cities in South America.

Methods. In this case-control study, we recruited young people, 15-16 and 20-24 years old, from the most deprived half of Bogotá (Colombia), Lima (Peru) and Buenos Aires (Argentina), who did and did not meet threshold criteria for depression and/or anxiety. Following multiple imputation for missing data, we used multivariable logistic regression to test whether cognitive and structural social capital were associated with case-control status, and we examined whether these were modified by socioeconomic status (SES).

Results. Amongst 2,402 young people (59.8% cases, 65.0% female), those with depression and/or anxiety were about half as likely to report living in areas with high cognitive social capital compared with controls (OR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.39, 0.66), with a trend in this direction for high versus low structural social capital (OR: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.59-1.03; p=.079). We did not observe effect modification by SES. 

Conclusion. Higher cognitive social capital was associated with reduced odds of depression and/or anxiety amongst youth in economically deprived, urban contexts in South America. This may offer an important community-based resource to promote youth mental health.

title: The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire: a German validation
description:
Curiosity plays an important role in early learning, but measures of trait curiosity in infancy and toddlerhood are still limited. The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ) was recently developed as a caregiver questionnaire for children aged 5 to 24 months and validated in a UK sample. The present study examined the ITCQ in a German sample to test its applicability in a different cultural context and to support cross-national research on early curiosity. 
291 German-speaking caregivers completed the German version of the ITCQ and a temperament questionnaire. Items targeted young children’s observable exploration behaviour and were evaluated on a 7-point Likert scale. Factor analyses indicated an overall acceptable fit of the original three-factor structure, although the Investigative subscale showed weaker fit and may require further refinement. We further observed mostly good internal consistency for the overall scale and subscales, good test-retest reliability, and curiosity was positively associated with Surgency and Effortful Control, while Negative Affect was largely unrelated to the curiosity dimensions except for a small negative association with Interactive curiosity.
Taken together, the findings largely replicate the original results and extend them to an independent German sample. They enable further research on trait curiosity in young children, both locally and across cultures, while also highlighting the importance of remaining attentive to culture-specific nuances. More broadly, the current results provide a solid foundation for future work on how curiosity develops and shapes learning across early childhood.

title: Demand or Relief? The Contingencies of Digital Disconnection and Well-Being at Work
description: Due to high demands of digital media, workers engage in digital disconnection, the deliberate non-use of digital technologies. This study investigates disconnection effects on affect, energy, stress, emotional exhaustion, connectedness, and loneliness. It introduces a (dis)connectivity demands framework with three factors: 1) work as a source of digital connectivity demands 2) salience of digital connectivity as a demand from disconnection, and 3) autonomous motivation as a (dis)connectivity resource. This two-week experience sampling study with N = 171 workers and T = 7,039 measurements finds that in situations with more disconnection participants reported more energy and less loneliness. Contrary to the hypotheses, disconnecting was associated with more stress. This effect depends on (dis)connectivity demands. Exploratory analyses show the need to account for multiple (dis)connectivity because more demands tended to predict less disconnection benefits. Cross-lagged associations show that disconnecting predicts subsequently higher energy. Emotional exhaustion and stress were followed by less disconnection.

title: Visual and verbal thought tendencies shape working memory under distraction
description: Working memory (WM) is a flexible function that may retain information through various representational routes, like detailed visual traces or abstract semantic codes. However, it is unclear whether both routes are equally suited to support WM performance and resilience to competition from sensory input. Here, we tested the flexibility and function of WM representational formats through three complementary lenses: model-derived stimulus memorability, individual variability in imagery, and task competition. Participants (N = 246) completed a WM task and a battery of imagery questionnaires. The task probed delayed-recognition for naturalistic images when task-irrelevant visual input appeared during maintenance. We found that imagery tendencies interacted with stimulus and task factors. For instance, memorable items were robust to imagery and visual distraction, but less memorable items were vulnerable to distraction—especially in individuals with stronger visual imagery. The findings highlight how multiple routes to WM maintenance may carry different costs in the face of competition.

title: Asian American Mythology and Pathways to Solidarity
description: Asian Americans in the U.S. are often considered the ‘model’ minority due to their perceived success compared to other racial minority groups. However, this mythology creates barriers for Asian Americans in fostering solidarity with other racially marginalized groups (i.e., intra-minority solidarity) and with Asian Americans of different ethnic backgrounds (i.e., inter-ethnic solidarity). One barrier is the presumption that Asian Americans do not experience racial discrimination, suggesting racism no longer exists. Another is the erasure of the ethnic diversity of Asian Americans, ignoring the experiences of some ethnic subgroups. We argue that raising awareness about Asian Americans’ historical and contemporary experiences that contradict the model minority myth can overcome these barriers. Learning that Asian Americans have and currently experience racism can promote intra-minority solidarity. Highlighting ethnic variation in immigration patterns and experiences can promote inter-ethnic solidarity. Critically, myth-busting of this kind can create collective action movements across U.S. racial groups.

title: Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement
description: Well-chosen covariates boost the design sensitivity of individually and cluster-randomized trials. We provide guidance on covariate selection generating an extensive compilation of single- and multilevel design parameters on student achievement. Embedded in psychometric heuristics, we analyzed (a) covariate types of varying bandwidth-fidelity, namely domain-identical (IP), cross-domain (CP), and fluid intelligence (Gf) pretests, as well as sociodemographic characteristics (SC), (b) covariate combinations quantifying incremental validities of CP, Gf, and/or SC beyond IP, and (c) covariate time lags of 1–7 years, testing validity degradation in IP, CP, and Gf. Estimates from six German samples (1,868 ≤ N ≤ 10,543) covering various outcome domains across Grades 1–12 were meta-analyzed and included in precision simulations. Results varied widely by grade level, domain, and hierarchical level. In general, IP outperformed CP, which slightly outperformed Gf and SC. Benefits from coupling IP with CP, Gf, and/or SC were small. IP appeared most affected by temporal validity decay. Findings are applied in illustrative scenarios of study planning and enriched by comprehensive Online Supplemental Material.

title: Quest for Significance is Linked to Power Motives: Correlational and Experimental Evidence
description: Drawing on dual perspectives on social hierarchies, we investigated the relationship between quest for significance and the motivation to gain power, as well as their causal links. Studies 1 and 2 found that quest for significance is positively associated with the motivation to gain power in long-term life goals, and in desired rank positions in power hierarchies. Quest for significance was also linked to greater discrepancies between current and desired power, and with dominant behavior. Studies 3 and 4 investigated the causal effects of quest for significance on power motives. Situationally induced significance loss (vs. high significance) increased the motivation to prevail in interpersonal interactions, a marker of exerting power, but did not affect long-term power goals nor desired societal power rank. Together, these findings suggest that when social worth is threatened and upward mobility within status hierarchies is difficult, individuals may pursue power as an alternative route to ascend in social hierarchies.

title: On the External Validity of Single-Case Designs: A Bayesian Approach
description: When selecting interventions for students or clients, practitioners typically need to estimate the probability that it will lead to socially significant changes in behavior. One potential solution to address this issue involves computing the conditional probability of success given prior experience and the outcomes observed in the research literature. The purpose of the study was to use Bayesian inference, an approach that considers prior beliefs, to examine how research evidence combined with practical experience may be used to assess the external validity (i.e., generality across participants) of findings from single-case research. Our results present the mean posterior probability with the high-density intervals for practitioners with different levels of experience. Relying on more research evidence and on more practical experience to make decisions tends to improve success rate estimates. Given that research on the topic remains limited, we argue that our proposal should not be viewed as immutable, but rather as a starting point for spurring further discussion and research on the topic.

title: When Social Ties Are Disrupted: Connectedness, Support, and Well-Being Across 49 Countries
description: Social connectedness is a fundamental predictor of psychological well-being, yet less is known about how disruptions in social relationships are linked to well-being across societies and whether received social support helps explain this association. The COVID-19 pandemic created a global context in which everyday social interactions were widely constrained, offering a unique opportunity to examine these questions. Using data from 16,685 participants across 49 countries, we investigated whether (a) received social support predicted well-being, (b) perceived changes in connectedness with family, friends, colleagues, and neighbors predicted well-being, (c) received social support mediated these associations, and (d) these relationships were consistent across countries. Multilevel and multilevel mediation analyses showed that higher received social support and increased connectedness across relationship domains were positively associated with well-being. Moreover, received social support partially mediated the association between changes in connectedness and well-being across family, friendship, workplace, and neighborhood ties. These patterns were broadly similar across countries. The findings suggest that both close and more distal social relationships contribute to psychological well-being partly because they facilitate access to support during periods of widespread disruption. More broadly, the results highlight the importance of maintaining social connection and support systems when normal patterns of interaction are constrained.

title: Mapping how LLMs debate societal issues when shadowing human personality traits, sociodemographics and social media behavior
description: Large Language Models (LLMs) can strongly shape social discourse, yet datasets investigating how LLM outputs vary across controlled social and contextual prompting remain sparse. Cognitive Digital Shadows (CDS) is a 190,000-record synthetic corpus supporting analyses of LLM-generated discourse. Each CDS record is generated by one of 19 LLMs, prompted to shadow either a human persona or an AI-assistant role. CDS contains LLM responses on 4 controversial societal topics: vaccines/healthcare, social media disinformation, the gender gap in science, and STEM stereotypes. Persona-conditioned records encode 17 sociodemographic and psychological attributes, providing data linking LLMs' prompts, language, stances and reasoning. Texts are validated for topic anchoring and can support emotional analyses via interpretable NLP (e.g. textual forma mentis networks). CDS is enriched by a pooling platform with user-friendly dashboards, enabling easy, interactive group-level comparisons of emotional and semantic framing across personas, topics and models. The CDS prompting framework supports future audits of LLMs' bias, social sensitivity and alignment.

title: Math Education Digital Shadows for facilitating learning with LLMs: Math performance, anxiety and confidence in simulated students and AIs
description: To enhance LLMs' impact on math education, we need data on their mathematical prowess and biases across prompts. To fill this gap, we introduce MEDS (Math Education Digital Shadows) as a dataset mapping how large language models reason about and report mathematics across human- and AI-like conditions. MEDS involves 28,000 personas from 14 LLMs (from families like Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Granite, Phi and Grok) shadowing either humans or AI assistants. Each record/shadow includes a set of prompts along with psychological/sociodemographic persona metadata and four types of math tasks: (i) open math interview, (ii) three psychometric tests about math perceptions with explanations, (iii) cognitive networks capturing math attitudes, and (iv) 18 high-school math test questions together with their reasoning and confidence scores. MEDS differs from traditional score-only math benchmarks because it integrates concepts of self-efficacy, math anxiety, and cognitive network science besides math proficiency scores. Data validation shows that the sampled LLMs exhibit schema integrity and consistent personas, together with family-specific peculiarities like human-like negative math attitudes, logical fallacies, and math overconfidence. MEDS will benefit learning analytics experts, cognitive scientists, and developers of safer AI tutors in mathematics.

title: Semantic characteristics do not influence spatialization in working memory
description: Serial order has been suggested to be represented spatially along a working memory line, oriented from left to right in Westerners. Such spatial coding of order is evidenced by the SPoARC (Spatial Positional Association of Response Codes), showing faster left-hand responses to early items in a sequence and faster right-hand responses to late items. Although this effect has been preferentially linked to semantic processing, the origin of the phenomenon remains unclear. In this study, we investigated the contribution of semantic content and semantic richness in the emergence of the effect. We asked 141 participants to perform a recognition task with stimuli whose semantic properties were manipulated using pseudowords, abstract words, and concrete words. We observed a spatialization effect using pseudowords, challenging the semantic hypothesis suggested in the literature. In addition, we did not detect any differences in spatialization between abstract and concrete words, suggesting that semantic richness does not influence this process. These results tend to indicate that semantic characteristics do not contribute to the emergence of spatialization in working memory. We suggest instead that the SPoARC would primarily stem from phonological processing.

title: Third-party punishment is common across human societies but varies with socioecology
description: Punishment systems are central to maintaining human cooperation, yet how they vary across societies remains poorly understood. Different theoretical frameworks make distinct predictions about who third-party punishment (3PP) defends and the socioecological conditions under which it occurs. We test such predictions using a new cross-cultural dataset of 3961 ethnographic texts (coded 11893 times) from 60 largely nonindustrial societies. We code evidence for second- and third-party punishment and, when third-party punishment is documented, whether it is enacted on behalf of kin, social partners, or the broader community. Using Bayesian multilevel regression models, we test preregistered hypotheses linking these different forms of punishment to society-level measures of complexity (i.e., technological and social differentiation, resource-use intensification, community size) and kinship intensity. We find that third-party punishment is widespread across societies and ethnographic texts, occurring more frequently than second-party punishment. Aggregated across relational subtypes, third-party punishment shows weak associations with socioecology; disaggregated, it shows distinct and theoretically meaningful patterns. Generalized 3PP on behalf of community members is positively associated with technological and social differentiation, while kin-directed 3PP is positively associated with kinship intensity and negatively associated with technological and social differentiation. Contrary to our prediction, partner-directed 3PP shows a robust negative association with resource-use intensification. Second-party punishment is negatively associated with technological and social differentiation. These findings show that socioecological structures shape not only the presence of punishment but also the forms it takes and whom it is used to defend, revealing distinct punishment regimes rather than a single enforcement continuum.

title: A cross-linguistic investigation of infant familiar word recognition across ages - The ManyBabies-AtHome: Looking-While-Listening project
description: The current study aims to examine the developmental trajectory of word recognition in infants learning different languages across different ages, using an online adaptation of the traditional Looking-While-Listening paradigm. Specifically, we aim to examine whether children’s word recognition as indexed by speed and accuracy of their looking toward a named referent varies as a function of (1) age of the child, (2) whether their caregiver indicated that they understand the word, and (3) the language they are learning. Infants between 10-24-months from various countries and learning various languages will be recruited by research teams across the world to participate in the study, with the goal of 48 infants for each language. Children will be presented with two familiar objects on the screen while hearing the label of one of the objects embedded in a carrier phrase. Additionally, caregivers will also report children’s knowledge of the presented words through a questionnaire. We predict that infant word recognition accuracy and speed will improve as they grow older. However, given the mixed evidence for convergence between parent reports and children’s word recognition, and the possibility that there may be variation in the relationship between caregiver report and performance across languages due to linguistic differences, the nature of the association between parental report of word knowledge or language background on children’s word recognition remains an open empirical question. With our approach, we aim to build a more inclusive model of studying infant word recognition, and to develop more resource-friendly adaptations for cross-linguistic research.

title: Mind wandering impedes statistical learning during  serial but not parallel visual search
description:
Mind wandering is a common mental state typically associated with task disengagement due to attention being shifted away from external stimuli (perceptual decoupling). However, recent work has proposed that reduced engagement of top-down executive control during mind wandering may facilitate automatic processes such as statistical learning. Here, we tested this possibility by assessing how mind wandering influences the extraction of spatial regularities during visual search. We conducted two experiments that differed in attentional demands: an attentive, serial visual search task (Experiment 1) and a pre-attentive, parallel visual search task (Experiment 2).
In experiment 1, forty-seven participants performed a probabilistic cueing task in which they searched for a T-shaped target among L-shaped distractors. Target locations were determined by a Markov chain such that one quadrant had a 70 % probability of containing the target, with the high probability quadrant dynamically determined by the location of the previous target, creating a probabilistic sequence of target locations. In experiment 2, fifty participants completed a similar task in which the target was a red dot among green dot distractors, minimizing the need for focused attention. In both experiments, participants intermittently reported their attention state via 20 thoughts probes, rating their current attentional focus from 1 (Completely on-task) to 10 (Completely off-task).
Across experiments, responses were faster when targets appeared in the high probability quadrant, which was also associated with a greater probability of a first saccade toward that location in experiment 1. Contrary to previous findings, however, mind wandering was associated with reduced statistical learning in the attentive search task (Experiment 1) and had no detectable effect in the pre-attentive search task (Experiment 2).
